newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: HEINEKEN FALL ON ANALYST DOWNGRADES.
newsitem.headline: HEINEKEN FALL ON ANALYST DOWNGRADES.

text.p: Shares in Dutch brewer Heineken NV fell to a seven-month low on Monday, driven down by a spate of downgrades after last week's shock profit warning, with analysts predicting more falls to come.
"It (Heineken stock) will go lower," said John David Roeg, analyst at Labouchere, adding he had downgraded the stock to a Sell from a Hold.

Heineken shares have plunged 16 percent or 58.70 guilders to 304.00 after last Friday's news of lower than expected first half profits and its warning that 1996 profits would fall short of 1995's 664 million guilders ($392 million).

"It could go as low as 250.00 to 275.00 guilders by the end of the year, perhaps sooner," said Roeg. The shares in June hit an all time high of 402.00 guilders, almost doubling in the 14 months from April 1995.

Heineken was at the forefront of this year's Amsterdam bourse surge, climbing on its perceived growth prospects which were punctured by a statement from chairman Karel Vuursteen last Friday that the 10 percent annual gains investors had enjoyed over the past six years could not be guaranteed.
Volumes in Heineken shares have ballooned from the usual 200,000 to 400,000 a day with one million changing hands by Monday afternoon. Over 3.7 million were traded on Friday.
Analysts warned even more froth would be blown off the shares, taking their drop earlier on Monday below 300.00 guilders to a seven month low of 294.00 guilders.
MeesPierson analyst Darrell Duthie, who also downgraded the stock to a Sell from a Hold, said the bottom was hard to call.

"If you look at 22 times (earnings per share) estimates for 1996 the share price comes in at 285.00 guilders, but I think it could even go below that, it hasn't got the same growth story as before," he said.
"If you assume 20 times estimates you get a price of 260.00 guilders," he added, saying this was possible before the end of the year but may be reached in the next few months or weeks.
The problem for the world's most international brewer lies in a saturated European beer market, where Heineken racks up over 70 percent of its sales at present.
And with cooler summer weather this year prompting European beer drinkers to leave their tipple on ice, sales will be particularly hard hit in 1996 overall.

But analysts agreed that Heineken's leading market position in many European countries, recent acquisitions in France which are expected to contribute to net profit in around three years time, and strong investment in South East Asia, meant the brewer's problems may be relatively short-lived.

"My feeling is the long term story for Heineken is still a very good one," said MeesPierson's Duthie. "They have a very strong position in European markets, their investments in Asia are going apace and they're in a good position in the U.S."
He expected profit growth in 1997 and 1998, giving fairly good average profit growth over five years.

ING Barings analyst Gerard Rijk, who downgraded his recommendation to Hold from Buy, said Heineken was in a period of transition. "A big part of their business is in mature markets and investing in new markets takes time."
